newsitem.title: CHINA: Taiwan-Cambodia talks continue, boycott threatened.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan-Cambodia talks continue, boycott threatened.

text.p: Taiwan said on Thursday it was hopeful that Cambodia would agree to reverse a decision to close down Taipei's unofficial trade office in Phnom Penh, but threatened to boycott Cambodian trade and tourism if talks fail.
"Both sides are conducting relevant negotiations at this moment, but we have not reached a final agreement," Foreign Ministry spokesman Roy Wu told reporters.

Cambodian co-premier Hun Sen said on Tuesday that Taiwan's office in Cambodia must close, alleging it had a role in backing forces loyal to co-premier Prince Norodom Ranariddh, whom Hun Sen ousted in a coup on July 6.
Taiwan has demanded that Phnom Penh revoke its decision to close its trade office in Cambodia under threat of what officials called "drastic" countermeasures.
"If it (Cambodia) does not alter its unfriendly move, the government will suggest that Taiwan investors no longer invest in Cambodia and Taiwan tourists not visit there," Wu said.
"We hope this will not happen," he added.
Taiwan, the largest source of foreign investment in Cambodia, has categorically denied any involvement by its government or people in the conflict.
Taipei described Hun Sen's move as "unacceptable" and "ridiculous".
Chang Lin-chen, a politics professor at the National Taiwan University, said Cambodia was unlikely to be seriously concerned about Taiwan's threatened boycott.

"Though Taiwan is the number one investor in Cambodia, most of the investment is short-term, and speculative, so it doesn't benefit Cambodia that much. Cambodia does not have much to lose," Chang said.
Communist China, which has regarded Nationalist-ruled Taiwan as a renegade province since their 1949 civil war split, hailed Cambodia's decision to shut Taiwan's office.
"We welcome the closure ...," Foreign Ministry spokesman Tang Guoqiang said in Beijing. "We believe the Cambodian side will deal with this matter under the principle of one China."
Cambodia recognises Beijing, not Taipei, as the sole Chinese sovereign, but like most of the world's countries has cultivated brisk unofficial economic ties with Taiwan.

Beijing has rarely indicated opposition to such unofficial ties, limiting its squeeze of Taiwan to a diplomatic embargo. It was not clear whether its support for Phnom Penh's move signalled a new willingness to pressure Taiwan economically.
Hun Sen said Taiwan investors were not involved in the affair and they should continue business as usual.
He has alleged that unidentified Taiwanese, including a general, supported Ranariddh's forces before fighting erupted between troops loyal to the rival premiers on July 5.
Hun Sen said Beijing's embassy in Phnom Penh could look after the interests of all Chinese people in Cambodia, including those from Taiwan.
Taiwanese officials and analysts said they did not rule out the possibility that Beijing had a hand in Hun Sen's decision.
"This is an opportunity for Cambodia and mainland China to cooperate," said Chang.
"Cambodia needs the Chinese communists' support because it is trying to gain legitimacy, and China will try to isolate Taiwan at any opportunity," Chang said.
